title: Judas Rescues the Jews of Gilead and Galilee
sum: The rededication of the Temple brings no peace. The peoples around Judea turn on the Jews who live among them, and Judas strikes back: at the Idumeans, the sons of Baean and the Ammonites (5:1–8). Letters and messengers arrive from Gilead, east of the Jordan, and from Galilee, where Jews are besieged and dying. Simon takes three thousand men to Galilee, and Judas and Jonathan take eight thousand to Gilead. In a string of quick marches Judas breaks the sieges, takes and burns town after town, and brings the Jews of both regions back to Judea, so that "not one of them had fallen" (5:54).

Two commanders left behind to guard Judea disobey orders, attack Jamnia to "win a name", and are routed by Gorgias. The writer draws the moral: they "were not of the seed of those men by whose hand Israel was given salvation" (5:62). The chapter ends with Judas destroying Hebron's stronghold and the altars of Azotus.
readings: Read as rescue

The chapter is driven by cries for help (5:10–15), and its campaigns end in evacuations, not occupation (5:23; 5:45). Judas brings people home "with great joy" (5:23), and the march ends at Mount Zion with thanksgiving (5:54).
Read as holy war

The writer tells the campaigns in the words of Deuteronomy and Joshua: the ban (5:5), the offer of peace (5:48), the killing of every male (5:28; 5:51), the burning of idols (5:68). These are among the hardest passages in the book for modern readers.
Read as a family's claim

The defeat of Joseph and Azariah (5:55–62) teaches that God saves Israel through Mattathias's sons and no one else. Many scholars see here the book's purpose: to show that the Hasmonean house ruled by God's choice.

views.C: Catholic teaching reads these wars by the measure of legitimate defense. Rescuing besieged and dying Jews is a cause it accepts. But it also teaches that noncombatants and those who surrender must be spared, and that "every act of war directed to the indiscriminate destruction of whole cities" is a crime (Catechism 2313–2314). The killing of every male at Bosor and Ephron and the burning of the precinct at Carnaim (5:44) are reported in the book, not commended to Christians.
views.O: Orthodox canon law honors those who defend the weak but treats killing in war as a stain. Basil the Great wrote that the fathers did not count killing in war as murder, yet advised that soldiers with blood on their hands keep away from communion for three years (Letter 188, Canon 13). Orthodox readers can admire Judas's rescue of his people and still mourn the slaughter.
views.P: Protestant churches place 1 Maccabees among the Apocrypha. Anglicans read it "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not to set doctrine (Thirty-nine Articles, Article VI); Luther's Bible called such books profitable and good to read; the Reformed give them no more weight than "other human writings" (Westminster Confession 1.3). All of them therefore feel free to judge Judas: his rescue of the Jews of Gilead is an example of courage, but the book's approval of the ban and the killing of every male is not binding.
views.H: Historians date these campaigns to 163 BC. Bar-Kochva reads them as fast rescue raids by a small army, which could not hold land so far from Judea. The account is shaped by the writer's models: Joshua's conquest, Deuteronomy's law of war and the judges. Many scholars think it was also written to give the later Hasmonean conquest of Idumea, Galilee and Transjordan (Josephus, Antiquities 13) a past.
views.J: Josephus retells the campaigns closely (Antiquities 12.327–353). The rabbis hardly mention them. What Jewish worship kept is a theme, not the battles: the Hanukkah prayer Al ha-Nissim thanks God for handing the many over to the few and the strong to the weak, which is the story of this chapter.

deep.b:
The writer tells Judas's campaigns in the language of Israel's old law of war. The sons of Baean are put "under the ban" (5:5), the Septuagint's word for herem, which Deuteronomy commands only for the peoples of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:1–2; Deuteronomy 20:16–18). At Ephron, Judas offers peace first, as Deuteronomy 20:10 requires, and only after the town refuses does he kill every male (5:48–51; Deuteronomy 20:13). At Azotus he burns the idols, as Deuteronomy 7:5 says. The march home ends at Zion with no one lost, like the count after the war with Midian (5:54; Numbers 31:49).

The book does not say that God commanded these wars. No prophet speaks, and the writer himself says there was none in those days (4:46; 9:27). He shows Judas obeying the written law, and lets that stand as his warrant. Modern readers notice what the law also allowed: the death of men who had laid down their arms (5:43–44). Josephus retells all of it without comment; Christian moral teaching has judged it more severely (see the views above). Whether Christians may fight in war at all is carded at Deuteronomy 20, and whether Joshua's wars give any warrant is carded in the Joshua introduction.

Chapter 5 begins with Jews under attack by their neighbors (5:1–2, 9–15), and its two campaigns end with refugees brought home: from Galilee and Arbatta (5:23), and from Gilead "from the least to the greatest" (5:45). Judas does not try to hold Gilead or Galilee, and he could not have done so. Most historians therefore call these rescue operations.

But the book was written a generation or two later, when the Hasmoneans had conquered Idumea and Samaria (under John Hyrcanus), part of Iturea in the north (under Aristobulus I) and much of the coast and the land east of the Jordan (under Alexander Jannaeus) (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254–258, 275–281, 318–319, 395–397). For those readers, chapter 5 showed that Jews had lived and suffered in those lands long before, and that Judas had already fought there. That is why some scholars read the chapter as background for Hasmonean rule. The two readings do not exclude each other: a true story of rescue can also serve a later claim.

echoes: Deuteronomy 20:10–18; Deuteronomy 7:1–5; Deuteronomy 2:26–30; Numbers 21:21–24; Numbers 31:49; Joshua 6:21; Joshua 8:28; Judges 7:16; 1 Samuel 11:11; 1 Samuel 14:6; Genesis 11:4; Isaiah 9:1; Psalm 83:4–8; 2 Kings 23:15

settings.by: The Jews who had fled to the stronghold of Dathema
settings.when: 163 BC, when the nations of Gilead gathered to destroy them (5:9)
settings.why: To beg for rescue before the stronghold fell, and to report the killing of a thousand Jews in the district of Tobias.
settings.readers: The book's first readers lived when Gilead and Galilee had become Hasmonean land: John Hyrcanus took Idumea and Samaria, Aristobulus I part of Iturea in the north, and Alexander Jannaeus ruled towns on the coast and east of the Jordan (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254–258, 275–281, 318–319, 395–397). The letter reminded them that Jews had lived in those regions before the conquest, and had cried to Judea for help.
views: Most historians, with Bar-Kochva, take the letter and the campaigns as real: brief rescue raids by an army too small to hold land.
Others think the writer arranged the story to give the later Hasmonean conquests a precedent.

Most date 1 Maccabees between about 130 and 100 BC, since it ends with John Hyrcanus's reign and mentions its chronicle (16:23–24). Its warm praise of Rome (chapter 8) points to a date before Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. A few scholars have argued that the last chapters were added later.

settings.by: Messengers from Galilee, with their clothes torn
settings.when: while the Gilead letter was still being read (5:14)
settings.why: To report that Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon and Galilee's foreign towns had joined to destroy the Jews there.

settings.to: His brother Simon, and then Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah
settings.when: after the great assembly decided to help (5:16)
settings.why: To send Simon to Galilee, to take Gilead himself with Jonathan, and to forbid the commanders left in Judea to start a battle. The order prepares for their disobedience in 5:55–62.

settings.when: at dawn, as the enemy attacked the stronghold (5:30–31)
settings.why: To send them into battle for their besieged kinsmen.

settings.when: when Timothy camped at Raphon with a new army
settings.why: To warn him that all the nations around, with hired Arabs, had gathered there.

settings.when: as Judas came near the stream at Raphon
settings.why: To set a sign: if Judas dared to cross first, he would win; if he held back, they would attack. It recalls Jonathan's sign at Michmash (1 Samuel 14:9–10).

settings.when: before he crossed the stream at Raphon
settings.why: To send every man into battle and leave no one in camp.

settings.when: when the town shut its gates against the returning column
settings.why: To ask for passage in peace, promising to harm no one.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the law heard Moses' request to Sihon (Numbers 21:22; Deuteronomy 2:27–28) and Deuteronomy's rule to offer peace before attacking a town (Deuteronomy 20:10). The message shows Judas keeping that rule before Ephron's refusal brings the law's harsh sentence (5:51; Deuteronomy 20:13).

settings.by: Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah
settings.when: while Judas and Simon were away, in 163 BC
settings.why: To win fame like Judas's by attacking Jamnia, against Judas's order (5:19). The writer echoes the builders of Babel, who wanted a name for themselves (Genesis 11:4).

title: The Death of Antiochus and the Battle of Beth-zechariah
sum: Far to the east, Antiochus IV fails to plunder a rich temple in Elymais and turns back. News reaches him that his armies in Judea have been routed and that the altar's abomination has been torn down. He falls sick with grief and, before he dies, confesses to his Friends that his troubles came on him because of what he did in Jerusalem (6:1–13). He names Philip regent, but Lysias makes the boy Antiochus V king (6:14–17).

When Judas besieges the Citadel, its defenders appeal to the new king. A huge royal army comes up with thirty-two war elephants. At Beth-zechariah Judas's brother Eleazar kills the tallest elephant, thinking the king is on it, and dies crushed beneath it (6:43–46). Judas falls back, Beth-zur surrenders in a Sabbath year, and the Temple is besieged until news of Philip's coup forces Lysias to make peace. The king grants the Jews their own laws, then breaks his oath and pulls down the Temple's walls (6:55–63).
readings: Read as judgment

Antiochus's own words state the book's view of history: "because of these things these troubles have found me" (6:13). The persecutor dies in grief in a foreign land, as Daniel had foretold the end of the arrogant king (Daniel 11:45).
Read as a turning point
Peace is made on the terms the revolt began with: "Let us grant that they may walk by their own laws, as before" (6:59). Religious freedom is won, but the Hasmonean struggle for power goes on.

views.C: The Roman lectionary reads 6:1–13 on a weekday in late autumn (Saturday of the thirty-third week, Year I) as a lesson in God's justice, before the Gospel of the resurrection. On Eleazar, Ambrose held him up as an example of courage that seeks the common good, not one's own life (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40.207).
views.O: The Orthodox Church counts 1 Maccabees as Scripture. Its feast of the Holy Maccabees on 1 August honors the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, not the warriors of this book. Cyril of Jerusalem taught those preparing for baptism that the little horn of Daniel 7 is the Antichrist still to come (Catechetical Lecture 15), so the persecutor of this chapter is not, for him, the last enemy.
views.P: Protestant interpreters used this chapter to read Daniel. Calvin's commentary on Daniel follows the history of Antiochus from the books of the Maccabees, while denying them the authority of Scripture, and Luther wrote that 1 Maccabees helps in understanding Daniel 11 (Preface to 1 Maccabees, 1533).
views.H: Three accounts of Antiochus's death survive: this one, the two in 2 Maccabees (1:13–16; 9), and Polybius's (Histories 31.9). A Babylonian tablet (BM 35603) dates the news of his death to late 164 BC. The battle of Beth-zechariah is one of the few defeats the book admits; historians trust its war details, though not its numbers.
views.J: Josephus, who knew Polybius, sided with this book: Antiochus died for what he did at Jerusalem, not for a temple he never managed to rob (Antiquities 12.358–359). The medieval Megillat Antiochus, read in some communities at Hanukkah, remembers Eleazar among the sons of Mattathias who fell in the war.

deep.h: Three deaths of Antiochus, and Daniel
deep.b:
Antiochus IV died in 164 BC, in the east. The sources agree on that and on little else. Here he fails to rob a temple in Elymais, hears of his defeats in Judea, and dies of grief, confessing his crimes in Jerusalem (6:1–16). In 2 Maccabees 9 God strikes him with a pain in his bowels as he rushes to make Jerusalem a graveyard; he falls from his chariot, rots alive and vows in vain to become a Jew. In 2 Maccabees 1:13–16, a letter says the priests of Nanea killed him in her temple. Polybius says only that he went mad after trying to rob a temple of Artemis in Elymais (Histories 31.9).

Daniel 11:40–45 had foretold the end of the arrogant king "between the seas and the beautiful holy mountain", which most critical scholars take to mean in the land of Israel. Antiochus died in Persia. For those scholars this shows that Daniel 11 was written before his death, accurate up to about 165 BC. Jerome, answering Porphyry, read Daniel 11:36–45 of the Antichrist, of whom Antiochus was a figure (Commentary on Daniel). Whether Antiochus is Daniel's little horn, or whether Daniel looks past him, is the card below.

Eleazar Avaran, Judas's brother (2:5), runs through the phalanx, gets under the tallest elephant and kills it, and it falls on him (6:43–46). The writer gives his motive: "He gave himself to save his people and gain an everlasting name for himself" (6:44). He was wrong about the king, who was not on that elephant, and the battle was lost anyway (6:47).

Christian readers have nearly always praised him. Ambrose wrote that he went under the beast and won an everlasting name, and he set Eleazar beside the martyrs as an example of courage (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40.207–208). Augustine's strict rule against killing oneself (City of God 1.21–26) was aimed at those who seek death to escape suffering or shame, and moral theologians have generally not applied it to a soldier who accepts certain death to save others. Medieval art made him a figure of Christ, who gave himself for his people: the Speculum humanae salvationis (1300s) sets Eleazar stabbing the elephant beside the Crucifixion (chapter 24).

Josephus tells the story twice. The Antiquities says that he died after first killing many of the enemy (12.373–374); the Jewish War is cooler, saying that he only attempted great things and showed that he preferred glory to life (Jewish War 1.42–44). Modern readers often compare him to Samson (Judges 16:30), and to Razis, who killed himself rather than fall into enemy hands (2 Maccabees 14:37–46). 1 Maccabees does not call Eleazar a martyr. He dies in battle, not for refusing to break the law, and the book keeps the two kinds of death apart (compare 2:29–38).

echoes: Daniel 11:40–45; Daniel 8:23–25; Daniel 7:8; Daniel 7:21–26; Isaiah 14:12–20; Genesis 41:42; Esther 8:2; Leviticus 25:1–7; Exodus 23:10–11; Judges 16:30; 1 Samuel 31:4; John 15:13; Joshua 9:15–20

settings.to: All his Friends, the high officials of his court
settings.when: 164 BC, as he lay dying in Persia
settings.why: To confess that his troubles came from the evil he did in Jerusalem, and to prepare the handing over of the kingdom (6:14–15).
settings.readers: The book's readers could set this speech beside other accounts. 2 Maccabees 9 makes Antiochus vow to free Jerusalem and become a Jew. Polybius blames his madness on an attempt to rob a temple in Elymais (Histories 31.9). Josephus, who knew Polybius and this book, judged the Jewish account more likely (Antiquities 12.358–359). Ancient historians composed speeches of this kind for their characters, and the words are the writer's: the enemy is made to confess the book's own view of history.
views: Some Christian preachers took the speech as true remorse that came only when death was near.
Many commentators note that he never names God or asks forgiveness, and read it as regret, not repentance.
Most historians treat the speech as a literary confession, not a record of his last words.

settings.when: 164 BC, after his failure at Elymais
settings.why: To tell the king that his armies had been routed, that Lysias had been driven back, and that the Jews had torn down the abomination and walled the sanctuary and Beth-zur. The report brings on the grief of which he dies (6:8).

settings.by: Men who escaped from the besieged Citadel, with ungodly Israelites who joined them
settings.to: King Antiochus V and his court
settings.when: 162 BC, during Judas's siege of the Citadel (6:19–21)
settings.why: To complain that loyalty to the king had cost them their lives and lands, and to warn him that Judas would grow stronger if he did not strike first.
settings.readers: Readers knew the Citadel's garrison and the Jews who sided with it (1:33–36), and knew how the story ended, when Simon took the Citadel and cleansed it in 141 BC (13:49–52). The speech lets those opponents state their own case: they had obeyed the king's decrees, and their own people treated them as enemies.

settings.by: Lysias, regent for the young king
settings.to: The king, the army commanders and the troops
settings.when: 162 BC, when news came that Philip had seized the government in Antioch (6:55–56)
settings.why: To end the siege quickly and give the Jews back their laws, so that the army could return to deal with Philip.
settings.readers: Readers knew that the peace was real and was broken almost at once (6:62). 2 Maccabees 11:22–26 gives a royal letter in the young king's name restoring the Temple and the Jews' customs, and many historians think that letter belongs to this peace. Lysias's admission, that the Jews fought "over their laws, which we did away with", gives the book's own view of the war's cause in the enemy's mouth.

traditions.q: Antiochus IV dies far from Jerusalem (6:1–16). Is he the "little horn" of Daniel 7:8 and Daniel 8:9–12, and does Daniel 11:36–45 still speak of him, or of a later power? (Whether Daniel's "abomination" is Antiochus's altar is asked at 1 Maccabees 1; whether the Antichrist is the papacy, at Revelation 13.)
views: The horn of Daniel 8 is Antiochus; the little horn of Daniel 7 and the king of Daniel 11:36–45 are the Antichrist. Jerome, answering Porphyry, who held that all of Daniel 11 speaks of Antiochus, read Daniel 8 of Antiochus but Daniel 7 and Daniel 11:36–45 of the Antichrist (Commentary on Daniel). The Catechism teaches that before Christ comes a final trial will reveal "the Antichrist" (Catechism 675).

The horn of Daniel 8 is Antiochus; the little horn of Daniel 7 is the Turk. Luther's preface to Daniel takes the horn of Daniel 8 and most of chapter 11 as Antiochus, and reads the little horn of Daniel 7 as Muhammad's empire. In the preface he applied the willful king of Daniel 11:36 to the papacy.

Antiochus in Daniel 8, Rome after Daniel 11:36. Calvin read the little horn of Daniel 8 as Antiochus, but held that from Daniel 11:36 the prophecy passes to the Roman Empire, not to Antiochus and not to a single Antichrist at the end of time (Commentaries on Daniel).

Neither horn is Antiochus. Uriah Smith read the little horn of Daniel 7 as the papacy, and the horn of Daniel 8 as Rome, pagan and then papal, since Antiochus was too weak to fit a horn that grew so great (Daniel and the Revelation). Ellen White taught the same line of history.

Antiochus in Daniel 8, a future Antichrist in Daniel 7 and from Daniel 11:36. The Scofield Reference Bible takes Daniel 8:9–14 and 11:21–35 of Antiochus as a foreshadowing, and reads Daniel 7:8 and 11:36–45 of a future "willful king", the Antichrist of the tribulation. J. Dwight Pentecost sets out the same scheme (Things to Come).

title: Alcimus, the Hasideans and the Defeat of Nicanor
sum: Demetrius I escapes from Rome, seizes the throne and has Antiochus V and Lysias killed (7:1–4). Alcimus, a priest who wants the high priesthood, comes to him with the lawless men of Israel and accuses Judas. The king sends Bacchides with Alcimus, now high priest. A group of scribes and the Hasideans trust "a priest of the line of Aaron" and seek peace; Alcimus swears them an oath and then kills sixty of them in one day, and the writer quotes Psalm 79 over them (7:12–18). Bacchides kills more at Beth-zaith, and Alcimus rules the land with an army.

When Judas grows strong again, Demetrius sends Nicanor, who tries to seize Judas by treachery. Turned away, Nicanor mocks the priests at the Temple and swears to burn it. The priests pray for vengeance; Judas prays, recalling Sennacherib's army struck down by the angel. On the thirteenth of Adar Nicanor falls at Adasa, his army is destroyed, and his head and right hand are hung up near Jerusalem. The day becomes a yearly feast (7:43–49).
readings: Read as a warning
The Hasideans trusted a priest's pedigree and an oath, and died for it (7:14–16). For the writer, the lawful line of Aaron does not make a man faithful.
Read as the Temple's deliverance

Nicanor's threat against the house where God's name is called (7:35–37) brings the priests' prayer and Judas's prayer, and the answer comes in battle. The chapter ends with a festival, like Hanukkah (4:59) and Purim (Esther 9:20–28).

views.H: Historians date Demetrius's return to 162 BC and Nicanor's defeat to March 161 BC. 2 Maccabees 14–15 tells the same story with large differences: Nicanor first befriends Judas, and his threat is answered by a vision of Jeremiah. The Hasideans' reasons for making peace (7:13–14) suggest that, once the law was restored, some Jews no longer saw a reason to fight, which is why many historians read the revolt from here as a struggle for power as well as for the law.
views.J: Nicanor's Day was kept for centuries. It is listed in Megillat Ta'anit as the thirteenth of Adar, and both Talmuds tell the story of Nicanor's hand (Bavli Taanit 18b; Yerushalmi Taanit 2:12). Genesis Rabbah 65:22 tells how Yakim of Tseroroth mocked his uncle, the sage Yose ben Yoezer, as he was led to execution. Many scholars identify Yakim with Alcimus, and some think Yose was among the sixty killed (7:16).

deep.b:
Alcimus was a priest of Aaron's line (7:14), but not of the house of Onias that had held the high priesthood before the crisis. Josephus says Antiochus V had already named him high priest (Antiquities 12.385–387), and 2 Maccabees 14:3 says he had "defiled himself" earlier. The Hasideans, who had fought beside Mattathias (2:42), came to him first in peace because he was "a priest of the line of Aaron" (7:14) and because the law had been restored (6:59). He swore to them, and then killed sixty of them in one day (7:15–16).

The writer sets Psalm 79 over the dead. The psalm mourns the loyal ones (hasidim) whose blood was poured out around Jerusalem with no one to bury them (Psalm 79:2–3). Its Hebrew word is the Hasideans' own name. The point is clear: the Hasideans trusted the wrong priest, and God's choice lay with Judas's family (5:62). Some modern historians see the story differently: the Hasideans' peace shows that devout Jews did not all back the Hasmoneans, and the book is answering them. Who the Hasideans were is set out on their topic page.

After the victory at Adasa, the people "resolved to keep this day every year, on the thirteenth of Adar" (7:49). 2 Maccabees ends the same way, adding that it is "the day before Mordecai's day" (2 Maccabees 15:36), that is, Purim. So the date answered a threat against the Temple with a feast, as the thirteenth of Adar had once turned against Haman's plot (Esther 9:1).

The feast lasted at least into the first centuries AD. Megillat Ta'anit, an Aramaic list of joyful days on which fasting was forbidden, includes it. The Talmuds tell how Nicanor's thumbs and big toes were hung at the gates of Jerusalem (Bavli Taanit 18b). Later the thirteenth of Adar became the Fast of Esther, and Nicanor's Day was forgotten in Jewish practice, while Hanukkah lived on. Christians never kept it. The pattern of the chapter, a threat to the Temple, prayer, victory and a feast, is the pattern of Hezekiah's deliverance (2 Kings 19:14–36), which Judas's prayer recalls (7:41).

echoes: Psalm 79:1–3; Psalm 74:10–11; Psalm 74:18; 1 Kings 8:29–30; 1 Kings 8:43; 2 Kings 19:14–19; 2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36; Esther 9:1; Esther 9:20–28; Judges 3:11; 1 Samuel 17:51; 1 Samuel 17:54; Ezra 6:10; Jeremiah 7:11

settings.when: 162 BC, as he entered the royal palace
settings.why: To have Antiochus V and Lysias killed without seeing them, so that he would not be seen to order their deaths face to face.

settings.by: Alcimus and the lawless and ungodly men of Israel
settings.when: soon after he took the throne
settings.why: To win royal support: Judas has killed the king's friends and driven them from their land, and a trusted officer should come and punish him.

settings.when: as Alcimus and Bacchides came with an army
settings.why: To explain their trust: a priest of Aaron's line would not harm them.

settings.to: The scribes and Hasideans who came to him
settings.when: at their meeting
settings.why: To promise them safety. He broke it the same day (7:16).

settings.when: over the sixty Hasideans killed by Alcimus
settings.why: To show the psalm fulfilled in the slaughter of God's loyal ones and to mourn them.
settings.readers: Readers who prayed Psalm 79 in Hebrew heard "your loyal ones" (hasidekha) as the very name of the Hasideans. The quotation is shortened and its Greek is close to, but not the same as, the Septuagint psalm. That fits a writer who quoted the Hebrew psalm in a Hebrew book, which a translator later put into Greek.
views: The formula "as in the words that he wrote" treats the psalmist as a prophet whose words came true.
Some interpreters, ancient and modern, have dated Psalms 44, 74 and 79 to the Maccabean crisis. Most scholars date Psalm 79 to the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC and see 1 Maccabees reusing it.

settings.when: after the killings
settings.why: To declare that there was no truth or justice in Alcimus and Bacchides, who had broken their oath.

settings.when: 161 BC, when Nicanor came to Jerusalem
settings.why: To lure Judas to a meeting where he could be seized (7:29–30).

settings.when: when they showed him the sacrifice offered for the king
settings.why: To force the surrender of Judas by threatening to burn the Temple.

settings.when: standing before the altar and the temple after Nicanor's threat
settings.why: To ask God to defend the house he chose for his name, and to bring vengeance on Nicanor for his blasphemies.
settings.readers: The prayer borrows Solomon's dedication: the house where God's name is called, a place of prayer for his people (1 Kings 8:29–30, 43). For priests serving after 164 BC, who had cleansed the Temple only three years before (4:36–59), Nicanor's threat repeated Antiochus's defilement. Readers kept the day of the answer as a feast (7:49).

settings.when: 161 BC, before the battle, with three thousand men
settings.why: To ask God to destroy Nicanor's army as he destroyed Sennacherib's, because Nicanor had spoken against the holy place.
settings.readers: Readers knew the story of Hezekiah, when the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 Assyrians in one night (2 Kings 19:35). 2 Maccabees gives a longer prayer at the same battle that names Hezekiah (2 Maccabees 15:22–24), which shows that the comparison was part of how the victory was remembered. The prayer does not name God or Sennacherib, as the book generally avoids naming God.

title: The Treaty with Rome
sum: Judas hears about the Romans: mighty in war, loyal to their friends, conquerors of the Gauls, of Spain, of Philip and Perseus of Macedon, of Antiochus the Great and of the Greeks. They make and unmake kings, yet none of them wears a crown; three hundred twenty men meet in their council every day, and they entrust their rule to one man each year, without envy (8:1–16). Some of the report is wrong, but its picture is clear: Rome is strong and keeps faith.

Judas sends Eupolemus and Jason to Rome to make friendship and an alliance, to lift the Greek yoke from Israel. The Senate agrees, and the chapter gives the treaty, written on bronze: each side will help the other in war and give nothing to the other's enemies. A warning to Demetrius closes it: if the Jews complain again, Rome will fight him by sea and by land (8:17–32).
readings: Read as diplomacy
The chapter is a careful record of a real step: a small nation seeking a great power's protection. It sets out the treaty in full and shows why Judas trusted Rome.
Read beside the prophets

The prophets warned against trusting foreign powers (Isaiah 31:1; 2 Chronicles 16:7), and Daniel and Revelation picture Rome as a beast. Read beside them, Judas's treaty raises the question of where Israel's help comes from.
Read with hindsight
Within a century Rome took Jerusalem (63 BC), and within two and a half it destroyed the Temple (AD 70). Later readers could hardly read the praise in 8:1–16 without irony.

views.P: For Protestant readers, who do not take the book as Scripture, the treaty is an example to weigh against the prophets. Calvin read Daniel's fourth kingdom as Rome, and held that from Daniel 11:36 the prophecy passes from Antiochus to the Roman Empire (Commentaries on Daniel). Read that way, chapter 8 shows Judas making friends with the very power Daniel had foreseen.
views.H: Most historians accept that a treaty was made in 161 BC, and that its form, with its clauses on mutual aid, matches Roman treaties of the time. Gruen argues that Rome made such agreements easily because they cost nothing, and kept them only when it suited. The report of Rome contains errors (8:7; 8:15–16) that show the writer knew Rome by hearsay.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembered the treaty with mixed feelings. Josephus, who lived under Rome, retells it (Antiquities 12.414–419). A Talmudic saying counts twenty-six years in which Rome kept faith with Israel before it began to oppress it (Bavli Avodah Zarah 8b). In rabbinic writing Rome became Edom and Esau, the brother who hates Jacob.

deep.h: Rome in Jewish and Christian eyes
deep.b:
Chapter 8 is the earliest Jewish account of Rome that survives, and it is almost all praise. Rome is strong, keeps faith with friends, has no king and no envy (8:1–16). The writer gets some things wrong: Antiochus the Great was not captured (8:7), Rome had two consuls, not one ruler (8:16), and the Senate did not meet every day (8:15). These errors suggest a report heard from afar, perhaps from Judas's envoys.

Later Jewish and Christian writers saw Rome differently. Daniel's fourth beast, which devours the earth (Daniel 7:7, 23), was read by most of them as Rome, though critical scholars take it to be the Greek kingdoms. The Psalms of Solomon, written after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, call him "the sinner" who let foreigners go up to God's altar. Revelation pictures Rome as the beast from the sea and as Babylon, drunk with the blood of the saints (Revelation 13; Revelation 17). In the rabbis' writings Rome became Edom, the hostile brother.

The difference is largely one of time. 1 Maccabees was written while Rome was still a distant friend. Its praise of Rome is one of the main reasons scholars date it before 63 BC.

The prophets warned Judah's kings against seeking help from Egypt or Aram instead of God (Isaiah 31:1–3; 2 Chronicles 16:7–9), and the psalm says, "Do not rely on nobles" (Psalm 146:3). Yet Abraham had allies (Genesis 14:13), Solomon made a treaty with Hiram (1 Kings 5:12), and the oath to the Gibeonites was binding (Joshua 9:15–19). The line most readers draw runs between making a treaty and putting one's trust in it.

1 Maccabees approves Judas's treaty and has his brothers renew it (12:1–4; 14:16–24). 2 Maccabees, written for a different purpose, never mentions it and credits God alone with Nicanor's defeat (2 Maccabees 15:21–27). Rome sent no help when Bacchides came back and Judas fell (9:1–18).

The tension between the treaty and the prophets' warnings is set out on the topic page on alliances with foreign powers.

echoes: Daniel 7:7; Daniel 7:23; Daniel 11:30; Revelation 13:1–8; Revelation 17:1–9; Revelation 18:2–3; Isaiah 31:1–3; 2 Chronicles 16:7–9; Psalm 146:3; Hosea 7:11; Genesis 14:13; 1 Kings 5:12; Joshua 9:15; 1 Kings 12:4; Deuteronomy 4:2

settings.by: The writer, telling what Judas heard
settings.when: 161 BC, before the embassy
settings.why: To explain why Judas sought Rome's friendship: Rome was strong, kept faith with its friends and broke its enemies.
settings.readers: Readers lived when Jonathan and Simon had renewed the treaty (12:1–4; 14:16–24; 15:15–24) and Rome still seemed a distant protector. They had not yet seen Pompey enter the Temple in 63 BC. The errors in the report (8:7; 8:16) show how little Judeans knew of Rome first-hand.
views: Many scholars think the account goes back to what Judas's envoys or traders told him, which would explain its errors.
Others stress that the praise was shaped to defend the Hasmonean policy of friendship with Rome.

settings.what: The envoys' speech to the Senate
settings.when: 161 BC, in the council chamber
settings.why: To ask that the Jews be enrolled as allies and friends of Rome.

settings.what: The treaty and the warning to Demetrius
settings.to: The nation of the Jews; the last lines quote Rome's letter to Demetrius
settings.when: 161 BC, written on bronze and sent to Jerusalem
settings.why: To set out mutual aid in war on equal terms, with Rome left free to judge "as the occasion requires", and to warn Demetrius to stop oppressing Rome's new friends. The warning (8:31–32) is a separate letter, to Demetrius, quoted inside the treaty text.
settings.readers: Readers kept this text as a charter: the Hasmonean state had been recognized by Rome. Josephus gives a version of it (Antiquities 12.416–419), and its clauses are close to Roman treaties with Greek states of the period. Its Greek is a translation of a Hebrew translation of a Latin or Greek original, so its exact wording is not Rome's.
views: Most historians accept that a real treaty lies behind the text.
Some older scholars thought Rome would not have made a formal treaty with rebels against a friendly king, and saw the text as a later composition.
